chapter_title: A Bottle of Dew (Fables and Folk Tales)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.activity_title: Reading the Folk Tale Aloud — Part I

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.3): Rama Natha's belief and the sage's counsel — oral responses.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the folk tale genre and Sudha Murty as author. Invite students to share what they know about magic potions or get-rich-quick stories to activate prior experience.
Read Part I of the story aloud (p.1–3), pausing at key moments — Rama Natha's obsession, the sage's arrival, and the dew-collection instruction. Students follow in their textbooks.

Take up "Let us discuss" questions after Part I (p.3): what Rama Natha believed and how the sage responded. Students answer in pairs first, then share with the class. Teacher reinforces meaning through targeted prompts.

periods.teacher_notes: The story turns on Rama Natha's naïve belief in magic — establish this clearly during reading so the ironic ending lands. A common pitfall is rushing past the sage's precise conditions (solo work, no substitutes), which are the hinge of the whole plot. Students who engage with the prediction question tend to read Part II with sharper attention.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.5): why Rama Natha felt angry and how wealth was created — class discussion.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect I (p.6–7): complete the fill-in and True/False questions on Rama Natha's journey.

time_bands.activity: Read Part II of the story aloud (p.3–5), giving students turns to read paragraphs. Focus on Madhumati's role — her selling the banana crop and the accumulation of wealth over six years.
Discuss "Let us discuss" questions after Part II (p.5): why Rama Natha felt cheated when nothing happened to the copper vessel, and how he and Madhumati together created real wealth.
Draw out the sage's revelation — there was never a magic potion. Invite students to state in one sentence what lesson Rama Natha learned, and take two or three responses.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read Rama Natha's obsession with the potion in Part I, students will now see how six years of labour quietly produced genuine gold — Madhumati's box of coins. Watch for students who think Madhumati's contribution was incidental; the discussion should make clear she was a full economic partner. The homework fill-in and True/False tasks on p.6–7 reinforce this reading before the deeper reflection work.

periods.activity_title: Thinking and Reflecting — Sequence and Inference

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect I (p.6–7): sequence of events and True/False on characters' motives.
Let us think and reflect II (p.7): why the sage insisted Rama Natha work alone — inferential short answers.

time_bands.activity: Briefly revisit the story's ending — Madhumati producing the box of gold — to anchor the reflection work that follows.

Work through "Let us think and reflect I" (p.6–7) as a class: the True/False statements about Madhumati and the sage, the outcome-matching table, and the event-sequencing MCQ. Students write answers, then compare with a partner.

Move to "Let us think and reflect II" (p.7): take up the inferential questions — why the sage insisted on solo work, why a large plantation grew, and how Rama Natha came to believe there was no magic. Encourage students to use evidence from the story.
Consolidate by asking students to share the before-and-after contrast in Rama Natha's character (p.7 table). Take two or three responses and note the turning point.

periods.teacher_notes: Having now read both parts of the story, students are ready to move from recall to inference — why the sage's ruse was pedagogically wise. A common difficulty is the distinction between what Rama Natha did and what Madhumati did; the before-and-after table on p.7 is a useful anchor for this. Students who rush the sequence MCQ tend to guess rather than trace the dew-bottle scene step by step — slow them down by asking them to locate each event in the text.

periods.activity_title: Listening to Madhumati's Day — Sequencing Events

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.10): number Madhumati's seven banana-distribution events in correct order.

time_bands.activity: Set context: Madhumati has a large bag of bananas to share. Ask students to predict whom she might visit — this activates story knowledge and readies them to track sequence.
Students read the seven events listed in their textbooks (p.10) silently, then the teacher reads the transcript aloud at a steady pace while students number the events in order.
Read the transcript a second time at a slightly faster pace. Students verify or revise their numbering. Then check answers as a class, event by event.

Brief discussion: which of Madhumati's actions shows generosity, and which shows business sense? Students share in pairs, then two or three pairs report to the class. Teacher connects Madhumati's character back to her role in building the family's wealth.

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript follows a clear sequencing chain of seven events tied to Madhumati's banana distribution (p.36); students may confuse the two gifting-to-individuals events (the boy and the neighbour) since both involve small amounts. Reading the transcript at two paces — steady then slightly faster — builds the habit of focused listening. The follow-up discussion about generosity versus business sense enriches the character portrait students built while reading.

periods.activity_title: Speaking About Hard Work — Sounds of 's' and Structured Discussion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.10–11): read aloud words with /s/ and /z/ sounds, identify sound patterns.
Let us speak (p.11): structured partner discussion — meaning, importance, and advice on hard work.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the dual sound of the letter 's' using the word list on p.10–11 (sage, wisdom, surprise, trees). Teacher models each word; students repeat chorally, then identify whether the 's' makes a /s/ or /z/ sound in additional words the teacher says aloud.

Students work in pairs for the structured discussion on hard work (p.11), using the given sentence starters. Each pair addresses all three prompts — what hard work means, three reasons it matters, and three pieces of advice. Teacher circulates and nudges hesitant speakers using the provided phrases.
Three pairs share one idea each with the class. Teacher notes interesting reasons and advice on the board, drawing a brief connection to Rama Natha's and Madhumati's example from the story.

periods.teacher_notes: The phonics segment is short and purposive — students are not memorising rules but noticing a pattern they can carry into future reading. A common pitfall in the discussion task is students producing single-word answers; the printed sentence starters on p.11 are scaffolds, not optional, and teachers should insist they are used at least once by each partner. Box 2.6i of the NCF middle-stage pedagogy document is relevant here: quiet students from varying backgrounds benefit from the structured starter format.

periods.activity_title: Homophones, Connectors, and a Tongue Twister

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.8): fill in the paragraph using eight story words correctly.
Let us learn (p.8): match homophones in Column A with Column B and complete meanings.
Let us learn (p.9): match Column A phrases to Column B using connectors — because, before, as soon as, as.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.9): write four sentences each using a pair of homophones from the table.

time_bands.activity: Work through the vocabulary fill-in paragraph (p.8) together — students predict the best word from the box for each blank, then justify their choice by connecting the word back to its use in the story.
Introduce homophones using the Column A/B table on p.8. Teacher reads each pair aloud; students complete the missing meanings individually, then pairs compare answers before whole-class check.

Students work on the connector-matching task (p.9): read each Column A clause, select the correct Column B match, and write the full sentence with the appropriate connecting word. Three or four sentences are shared aloud to check logical coherence.
Quick close: teacher reads the tongue twister on p.9 at increasing speed. Students repeat. The exercise demonstrates how sound precision matters — a bridge to the phonics work from the speaking unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse homophones in writing by relying on sound alone — the Column A/B table on p.8 makes the spelling difference visible. In the connector task, watch for students who always choose 'because' regardless of the clause relationship; asking them to test 'as soon as' or 'before' first usually corrects this. The homework homophone sentences work best when students aim for humorous or surprising combinations, as in the textbook example.

periods.activity_title: Describing a Banana and Exploring Varieties

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.11–12): write eight sentences describing a banana using the word-map clues.
Let us explore (p.12): identify two or three banana varieties grown in India — brief group share.

time_bands.activity: Show students the word-map on p.11–12. Read each clue category aloud — colour, smell, taste, texture, when eaten, health benefit. Clarify any unfamiliar words before writing begins.

Pairs work on the descriptive paragraph task (p.11–12): draft eight sentences using the word-map clues, alternating sentences between partners. Teacher circulates, prompting specific sensory language.
Three pairs share their descriptions. Class notices what made each description vivid — the specific adjective chosen, the sensory detail selected. Brief peer appreciation round.

Introduce the "Let us explore" task (p.12): students brainstorm banana varieties they know — Robusta, Nendran, Red Banana, Poovan — sharing names from their own region. Teacher introduces the NHB resource as a research starting point for independent follow-up.

periods.teacher_notes: Having engaged with the banana plantation throughout the story, students bring genuine familiarity to this descriptive writing task — that lived context improves the specificity of their sentences. A common pitfall is that pairs default to listing rather than writing full, connected sentences; remind them to use each word-map clue as a prompt for one complete sentence. The beyond-text brainstorm at the close is intentionally brief — its purpose is to open curiosity about regional agricultural diversity, not to exhaust the topic.

periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis — Folk Tale, Labour, and Language

time_bands.activity: Open with a whole-class question: what makes 'A Bottle of Dew' a folk tale rather than a simple story? Students identify features — a wise figure, a lesson, a transformation of character — naming evidence from the text.

Rapid oral round: teacher reads five key moments from the story (the sage's instruction, Madhumati at the market, Rama Natha dropping dew on the copper vessel, Madhumati's box of gold, the sage's revelation). For each, students say in one sentence what it reveals about a character or the folk tale's central idea.

Students write a short paragraph (5–6 sentences) from Madhumati's perspective: how did she feel and what did she do across the six years? They use at least one connector (because, as soon as, before) and one homophone pair from the vocabulary work. Pairs swap and give one word of feedback.

Brief comparison discussion: how is the magic-potion story a form of wisdom teaching? Students connect the sage's ruse to other folk tales or stories they know where a wise person uses an indirect method to teach a lesson. Two or three students share examples.

Closing reflection: teacher asks students to name, without looking at the book, one word or phrase from the chapter that has stayed with them — from the vocabulary list, the story, or the discussion about hard work. This surfaces the language each student found most resonant.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws on all strands of the chapter — the folk tale's narrative arc, Madhumati's journey heard in the listening transcript, the phonics and homophone work, the descriptive writing, and the beyond-text curiosity about banana cultivation — without continuing or completing any earlier task. Students arrive with varied exposure depending on which units their class covered; the activities are designed to be accessible on the strength of the story alone. The Madhumati paragraph activates grammar in a genuine communicative context rather than as an isolated exercise.
materials: Textbook p.1–12 (full chapter available for reference)

items.item_stem: When the sage Mahipati told Rama Natha how to make the magic potion, he gave three specific conditions. Which of the following correctly states all three conditions the sage set?

options.label: A
options.text: Plant any crop, water it with river water, and bring the harvest to the sage each winter.

options.label: B
options.text: Plant banana plants, let others tend them, and collect dew over three years.

options.label: C
options.text: Plant banana plants, water them himself, and collect the morning dew from the leaves by hand until he had five litres.

options.label: D
options.text: Plant banana trees, hire workers to water them, and collect five litres of dew each morning.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student recalls the banana-planting and dew-collection but misses the sage's insistence that Rama Natha do all the work himself — a key condition of the ruse.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has generalised the task away from the specific crop and source, suggesting they read the instructions loosely rather than attending to exact wording.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student confuses the duration and misremembers the solo-work condition — likely recalling that time was involved but not the precise terms.

items.source_lo: Student retrieves and infers information from a folk tale narrative using prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Rama Natha's obsession with magic, the sage's dew-collection ruse, Madhumati's role in creating wealth over six years.
items.item_stem: The sage's instruction about the dew was a ruse — he never intended to enchant any liquid. What does the sage's choice to use a ruse rather than direct advice tell us about his understanding of Rama Natha's character? Support your answer with evidence from the story.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The sage understood that Rama Natha was so deeply obsessed with the idea of a magic potion that plain advice would have been ignored or dismissed. By giving him a task he believed would lead to magic, the sage ensured Rama Natha would actually work his land — and the years of labour produced real wealth, proving the sage's wisdom.

items.source_context: Madhumati's seven actions distributing bananas — to her mother, the market, Kalawati, a hungry boy, and her neighbour.
items.item_stem: Your teacher will read the account of Madhumati's day with her bananas aloud. Listen carefully, then answer: which TWO events happen before Madhumati goes to the market to sell the bananas?

options.text: Madhumati gives two bananas to a hungry boy on the way home.
Madhumati meets her old friend Kalawati in the market.
Madhumati sets off with many large bags of bananas.
Madhumati visits her mother and gives her two dozen bananas.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — Madhumati visits her mother and gives two dozen bananas before going to the market.
2. False — Madhumati meets Kalawati inside the market, which happens after she goes there to sell.
3. False — Madhumati gives two bananas to the hungry boy on the way home, which is much later in the sequence.
4. True — The account opens with Madhumati already holding many big bags of bananas, which is the starting state before any event.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Goes to the market = 1, Gifts Kalawati = 2, Gives boy two bananas = 3, Visits neighbour = 4.

items.item_stem: Think about Rama Natha's experience of working in the fields every day for six years. In two or three sentences, describe what 'hard work' means to you, using at least one of the following starters: 'It means…', 'It is something…', or 'What I mean is…'

expected_elements: Gives a personal definition of hard work in own words.
Uses at least one printed sentence starter correctly.
Speaks in complete sentences, not single words.
Connects the idea to effort or persistence — not just activity.

items.item_stem: Imagine a friend who keeps looking for shortcuts instead of putting in effort — just as Rama Natha did before meeting the sage. Give your friend three pieces of advice on why hard work matters, using the starters: 'Firstly, I feel… because…', 'Secondly, I think… since…', and 'Lastly, I believe… as…'. Speak for about one minute.

expected_elements: Three distinct reasons offered, not repetitions of one idea.
Each reason supported by a brief justification (because/since/as).
All three printed starters used in order.
Advice is practical and specific, not vague generalities.

items.item_stem:
The sentences below describe events from the story of Rama Natha and Madhumati. Choose the correct connecting word in brackets to complete each sentence so that it makes logical sense, and briefly explain why your chosen connector fits.

1. Rama Natha began cleaning his neglected fields __________ the sage told him the dew-collection method. (because / as soon as / before)
2. Madhumati sold the bananas at the market __________ she was a careful and enterprising partner. (because / before / as soon as)
3. Rama Natha felt cheated __________ nothing happened when he sprinkled the dew on the copper vessel. (as soon as / before / as)

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. as soon as — Rama Natha began the work immediately after the sage gave the instruction, showing a direct trigger relationship. 2. because — Madhumati's enterprise explains why she succeeded at selling. 3. as soon as — his feeling of being cheated arose the instant the copper vessel showed no change.

items.item_stem: In the story, Rama Natha grows a huge banana plantation. India is one of the world's largest producers of bananas, and many different varieties are grown across the country. Write a short paragraph (five to six sentences) naming at least two varieties of banana grown in India, mentioning one region where each is commonly found, and describing one way each variety is used — for eating fresh, cooking, or another purpose.

expected_elements: At least two named banana varieties mentioned (e.g., Robusta, Nendran, Poovan, Red Banana).
A region of India linked to each variety named.
One use stated for each variety — eating fresh, cooking, or another purpose.
Written in connected sentences, not a bullet list.
Information is accurate and not contradicted by common knowledge.

items.source_lo: Student extends learning beyond the text by researching a real-world topic connected to the story's setting.
items.source_context: Varieties of bananas grown and eaten across different regions of India — agricultural and cultural diversity.
items.item_stem: Design a simple research project to find out how banana farming has changed in one Indian state over the last twenty years. In your plan, state: (a) one question you want to answer, (b) two sources you would use to find information, and (c) how you would present your findings to your class. Also write one sentence explaining how your findings connect to the idea of hard work in the story of Rama Natha.

expected_elements: A specific, focused research question about banana farming in one state.
Two plausible sources named — government website, local farmer interview, library book.
A clear presentation format — poster, oral report, chart, or written summary.
A meaningful connection drawn between research findings and the story's hard-work theme.
